rows: Radcliffe Library, Oxford

Talbot photographed the round, domed Radcliffe Camera in Oxford in 1836, very early in his experiments with paper negatives. The soft gray picture shows how a famous building looked to the first camera users.
What shape is the building?
Tower at Lacock
Talbot photographed a tower at his home, Lacock Abbey, in 1837. The slow paper and chemicals gave the stone walls a soft, dreamy look.
Why do you think he photographed his own home?
Articles of China on Four Shelves
Talbot photographed the china on four shelves of a cabinet in 1839, to show that a camera could copy lots of small things at once. He said it was like having a record that nobody could argue with.
How many different shapes of plates and cups can you count?
Articles of Glass on Three Shelves
Here Talbot photographed glass bottles and decanters on three shelves. Glass was tricky because it shines and shows reflections, but the camera handled it well.
How do you think the light shows up in the glass?
Gate of Christ Church, Oxford
Talbot photographed a gate at Christ Church college in Oxford in 1839. It is one of his early calotype views and shows a building that is still there today.
What would you see if you walked through the gate?
View from Daguerre's House
This is a view from the window of Louis Daguerre's own house in 1839, the year he announced the daguerreotype. It shows the roofs and sky as Daguerre saw them.
What might Daguerre have been thinking when he looked out?
The Chalet
Joseph-Philibert Girault de Prangey photographed a wooden chalet in France in 1841. His daguerreotypes are some of the finest early views of buildings.
What is the roof made of?
Tour Saint-Jacques, Paris
Girault de Prangey photographed the Saint-Jacques tower in Paris in 1841. The tower is all that is left of an old church, and it still stands in the middle of the city.
Why do you think only the tower is left?
Notre-Dame de Paris before 1841
Vincent Chevalier made this daguerreotype of the front of Notre-Dame before he died in 1841. It is one of the oldest photographs of the cathedral.
What would you look for if you compared it with today's cathedral?
Hamburg's Fire Ruins from the Roof of the New Exchange
In 1842 a great fire burned much of Hamburg, Germany. Carl Ferdinand Stelzner photographed the ruins afterward, making these some of the first news photographs of a disaster.
Why would people want to see photographs of a fire?
Ruins of the Nikolai Church, Hamburg
Stelzner photographed the burnt walls of the Nikolai church after the great fire of 1842 in Hamburg. Photographs of disasters like this are among the first of their kind.
What parts of the church are still standing?
Notre-Dame, 1842
This round daguerreotype by Marc-Antoine Gaudin shows Notre-Dame in Paris in 1842. The image is reversed, as daguerreotypes were, like a mirror.
Why would a mirror-image picture be confusing?
Fountain Frozen by Frost
Girault de Prangey photographed a fountain in Paris that had frozen into ice in the winter of 1842. Frozen water stays still, which suited his slow camera.
Why is a frozen fountain easier to photograph than a running one?
The Burial of the Duke of Orléans

Marc-Antoine Gaudin photographed the funeral of Prince Ferdinand, Duke of Orléans, who died in a carriage accident in 1842. The crowd and the tall buildings around Notre-Dame show how big the event was.
Why would people photograph a funeral?
Maida, Sir Walter Scott's Favorite Dog
This is a stone statue of Maida, the dog of the author Sir Walter Scott, photographed by Talbot in 1844. The statue lies beside the doorway at Abbotsford, Scott's home in Scotland.
Why would someone make a statue of their dog?
Melrose Abbey
Talbot photographed the ruined Melrose Abbey in Scotland in 1844. The old walls and windows were a favorite subject for artists, and the calotype's soft look suited them.
What parts of the abbey are missing?
Scenery of Loch Katrine
Talbot photographed Loch Katrine, a famous lake in the Scottish Highlands, in 1844. Sir Walter Scott had made the lake famous in a poem.
How does the water meet the hills?
Thomas Starr King
Thomas Starr King was a minister and speaker who later helped keep California on the Union side in the Civil War. Mathew Brady photographed him in the 1840s.
What would you ask a famous speaker?
Michael Faraday
Michael Faraday was a scientist who discovered how electricity and magnets work together. His studio portrait was made around 1844 at the Brady studio.
What would you like to ask a scientist who studied electricity?
Joseph Story
Joseph Story was a justice of the U.S. Supreme Court. This daguerreotype was made in 1844 by the studio of Mathew Brady.
What do you think a judge thinks about?
Pierre Soulé
Pierre Soulé was a senator from Louisiana who was born in France. Brady photographed him in the 1840s.
How is his face different from the other politicians in Brady's gallery?
William McKendree Gwin
William Gwin was a senator from California who was born in Tennessee. His portrait was made by Brady in the 1840s.
What do you think a senator from the West wanted to look like?
Solomon Downs
Solomon Downs was a senator from Louisiana. Mathew Brady's portrait of him is one of hundreds of famous Americans photographed in the 1840s.
What details of his clothing do you notice?
The Optician Anders Krüss and Family
Hermann Biow photographed a family of opticians, makers of lenses, in Hamburg in 1845. Biow was a German photographer who made some of the earliest portraits in Germany.
What do lenses have to do with photography?
The Brothers Grimm
Hermann Biow photographed the Brothers Grimm in 1847. Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected fairy tales like Cinderella, Snow White and Hansel and Gretel.
Which Grimm fairy tale is your favorite?
Peter von Cornelius
Peter von Cornelius was a famous German painter. Hermann Biow photographed him in Berlin in 1847.
Why would a painter pose for a photographer?
Adolphsplatz, Hamburg
Stelzner photographed the Adolphsplatz in Hamburg in 1847. His pictures of the city are valuable because much of it was burned in the 1842 fire.
Which buildings do you think survived the fire?
Alexander von Humboldt
Alexander von Humboldt was a famous German scientist and explorer who traveled to South America. Hermann Biow photographed him in Berlin in 1847.
What would you like to ask an explorer?
John C. Calhoun
John C. Calhoun was a senator and vice president from South Carolina, and he strongly defended slavery. This daguerreotype of him was made by Brady in March 1849.
What can you tell about him from his stern look?
The Pavillon de Flore and the Tuileries Gardens
Marie-Charles-Isidore Choiselat photographed a wing of the Tuileries Palace and its gardens in Paris in 1849. The palace was burned down in 1871.
Why would a view of a lost building be valuable?
Cornelius Vanderbilt
Cornelius Vanderbilt was a shipping and railroad tycoon who became one of the richest people in America. This portrait was made by the Brady studio around 1849.
How do you think wealth showed in a portrait?
Roger B. Taney
Roger Taney was Chief Justice of the United States. Brady photographed him in 1849 as part of his collection of famous Americans.
What does a chief justice's face say about his job?
Martin Van Buren
Martin Van Buren was the eighth president of the United States. This daguerreotype was taken around 1849 by Mathew Brady's studio, after he left the presidency.
Which president would you like to photograph today?
Atelier Wehnert-Beckmann, Leipzig
Bertha Wehnert-Beckmann ran one of the first photography studios in Leipzig, Germany. This daguerreotype shows the glass-roofed room where she photographed her customers.
Why would a photo studio need so much glass?
The Propylaea, Acropolis, Athens
Baron Jean-Baptiste Louis Gros photographed the entrance to the Acropolis in Athens in May or June 1850. It is one of the earliest photographs of the Parthenon site.
Why would the Greeks care about the photograph?
Madame Hahn and Her Seven Children
J. Völlner photographed a mother with seven children in the mid-1800s. Family portraits like this were a point of pride, and a big family needed a big studio.
How many children can you count?
Nathaniel Parker Willis
Nathaniel Parker Willis was a popular American poet and magazine editor. Mathew Brady's studio photographed him in the 1850s.
What would a magazine editor like to read?
Château de Chenonceau, West Façade
Gustave Le Gray photographed the west side of this French castle in 1851. Chenonceau is built right over the River Cher, which makes it look as if it floats.
How is the castle different from most castles?
Château de Chenonceau, North Façade
Le Gray photographed the north side of Chenonceau in 1851. He and other photographers worked for the government to record old French buildings.
Why would the government want these pictures?
Château de Chenonceau, Detail
This close-up of Chenonceau by Le Gray shows the rooms of Queen Louise of Lorraine, a widow who lived there in the 1500s. The carved stone is crisp in the picture.
What details do you notice up close?
Château de Chenonceau
Le Gray made several pictures of Chenonceau in 1851. This one shows the long gallery stretching over the river, in sharp light.
How would you cross a river without a bridge, in a castle?
Cottages at Balaklava
Roger Fenton photographed small stone cottages in the town of Balaklava during the Crimean War. Soldiers and officers used buildings like these as quarters.
How might the soldiers have used these cottages?
Mortar Batteries in Front of the Picquet House
Fenton photographed rows of mortars, short guns that fired shells high into the air, near the front lines at Sevastopol. It is a picture of war made without any fighting in it.
Why couldn't Fenton photograph the fighting?
Cattle and Carts Leaving Balaklava
Fenton photographed carts and cattle moving out of the port of Balaklava. Everything the army ate had to be carried by animals, and that makes the picture busy.
What would you carry if you had to move an army?
Sevastopol, from the Mortar Battery
Fenton photographed the besieged city of Sevastopol from a mortar battery. The battered city lies in the distance, beyond the soldiers' guns.
What do you see in the distance?
Picquet House, Cathcart's Hill
Fenton photographed a house used by officers on a hill outside Sevastopol. Many of the buildings became the headquarters of soldiers.
Why would an army choose a hill?
Admiral Lord Lyons
Admiral Lord Lyons commanded the British fleet in the Black Sea during the Crimean War. Fenton photographed him in 1855 beside a small tent.
What does the admiral's uniform tell you?
Officers of the 42nd Highlanders
Fenton photographed officers of a Scottish regiment, the 42nd Highlanders, in the Crimea. They wear kilts and tall feathered caps even in a war zone.
Which part of the uniform seems the strangest for a war?
Cooking House of the 8th Hussars
Fenton photographed a rough outdoor kitchen built by cavalry soldiers in the Crimea. Food was scarce and cold weather was harsh, and cooks did their best.
What would you cook in a camp like this?
Amiens Cathedral
Édouard Baldus photographed the great cathedral of Amiens in France in a sweeping view. He pasted several negatives together to show the whole building.
How could he fit such a tall building in one picture?
Husband and Wife
You hardly ever see smiling portraits from the mid-1800s, because the sitter had to hold still and photographs were serious. This couple has a relaxed look, which makes it special.
Why is it hard to smile for a long time?
The Rhône Viaduct, Lyon
Édouard Baldus photographed a new railway bridge over the Rhône river in Lyon. He documented rail projects across France, and his pictures show iron and stone engineering at its best.
Why would a photographer be hired to photograph a bridge?
Husband
A man poses on his own. The photographer let him choose a relaxed look, and his face seems to be on the edge of a smile.
What would you do with your face for a portrait?
Caves of Karli: The Approach
William Johnson photographed the entrance to the ancient Karli caves in western India in 1855. The caves are carved from solid rock and were used by Buddhist monks.
How would you build a temple inside a mountain?
Ingenious Device
A photographer in Hong Kong made this picture around 1855, perhaps a playful scene showing a trick or a gadget. Photography studios in China were some of the first in Asia.
What do you think the device does?
Bois de Boulogne, Paris
Charles Marville photographed the Bois de Boulogne, a huge park on the edge of Paris that was redesigned in the 1850s and 1860s. His pictures show a landscape that was newly made to look natural.
What makes a park feel like nature?
Landscape
Henry White was a London lawyer and one of Britain's best landscape photographers in the 1850s. His fine pictures of trees and fields were praised at exhibitions.
What do you see in the trees?
Maneuvers, Camp de Châlons
Gustave Le Gray photographed soldiers drilling at the Camp de Châlons in 1857. The emperor Napoleon III wanted to show off his army's training.
How do soldiers practice?
Daniel Maclise
Daniel Maclise was an Irish painter who worked in London. William Lake Price photographed him next to a painting, which was a way of showing an artist with his work.
Why would a painter pose beside his own painting?
Cavalry Maneuvers, Camp de Châlons
Le Gray photographed horse soldiers practicing at the camp in Châlons, France. Moving horses were hard to capture, so the picture shows a very good camera and quick work for 1857.
Why are horses harder to photograph than tents?
Zouaves, Camp de Châlons
The Zouaves were French soldiers known for their colorful uniforms inspired by North Africa. Le Gray photographed their quarters at the camp in 1857.
Why might a soldier like a bright uniform?
The Iron Bridge, Lucknow
Felice Beato photographed an iron bridge in Lucknow, India, in 1858, after a long uprising against British rule. Beato was one of the earliest war photographers.
What is the bridge crossing?
The Small Imambara, Lucknow
Beato photographed the Chota Imambara, a beautiful shrine in Lucknow, India. It has a golden dome and tall arches, and it was damaged in the fighting.
What features make it look like a shrine?
Gateway to the Residency, Lucknow
Beato photographed the gate of the British Residency in Lucknow after the siege in 1858. The walls still show damage from the fighting.
What damage can you see?
Perumal Temple Vimana, Madurai
Linnaeus Tripe photographed the tower of the Perumal Temple in Madurai from a corner of its court. He worked there in 1858, and the temple would have been crowded with worshippers.
Where are all the people in this picture?
Great Temple Walls, Madurai
Tripe photographed the walls of the Great Temple in Madurai, one of the biggest temples in India. The photograph is taken from a corner so that you can see the stone steps and the carved base.
How many levels does the wall have?
Pudhu Mandapa, Madurai
Tripe photographed a long hall of stone pillars in Madurai, built by Tirumal Nayak in the 1600s. Every pillar is carved with figures of gods, riders and animals.
What kinds of figures can you find on the pillars?
Entrance to the Minakshi Temple, Madurai
Tripe photographed the entrance gateways of the Minakshi Sundareshvara Temple in Madurai, India. The gateways grow higher the farther they stand from the center.
Which gateway is the tallest?
Buland Darwaza, Fatehpur Sikri
John Murray photographed the huge gateway of the Great Mosque at Fatehpur Sikri, built by the Mughal emperor Akbar. A person stands in front to show how big it is.
How big is the person compared with the gate?
Exterior of the Secundra Bagh
Felice Beato photographed the outside of the Secundra Bagh, a walled garden in Lucknow where a battle took place in 1857. His pictures show the broken walls afterward.
What would the garden have been like before the battle?
Gate of the Small Imambara, Lucknow
Beato photographed a damaged gateway of the Chota Imambara, a shrine in Lucknow, after the siege in 1858. The beautiful carved stone shows signs of war.
How can a beautiful building be damaged by war?
Hindu Rao's House, Delhi Ridge
Beato photographed a house on the ridge above Delhi that was damaged during the siege in 1857. It was a stronghold for British soldiers.
Why would a house on a hill be useful in a war?
Lesser Court of the Residency, Lucknow
Beato photographed a courtyard of the Residency in Lucknow, where a British brigadier was killed during the siege. The broken walls show how the fighting went on.
What do the broken walls tell you?
Major Desborough
Felice Beato photographed Major Desborough around 1858 to 1860 on his travels in Asia. Beato made portraits of soldiers and officials as well as landscapes.
What does the major's uniform tell you about him?
The Tiber, Tuileries Garden
Charles Nègre photographed a statue called the Tiber in the Tuileries Gardens in Paris. In 1859 the government paid him to take 50 photographs of the garden's statues.
What river do you think the statue stands for?
Prison Hall, Stereograph
This 3D stereocard shows the inside of a prison hall in the United States in 1860. Stereocards like this were sold to people who could not travel.
Why would people buy pictures of faraway places?
Mount Maudit, Savoy
The Bisson brothers photographed Mont Maudit in the Alps, one of the great peaks of Europe, in the 1860s. They carried a mule-load of glass plates up the mountain.
Why did they carry so many glass plates?
Floral Still Life
Charles Aubry made close-up photographs of leaves and flowers, which designers used as models. This arrangement shows how carefully he looked at plants.
Which flower do you like best?
Road in the Forest
Eugène Cuvelier was a painter and photographer who worked in the forest of Fontainebleau in France. His soft pictures of forest paths look like paintings of the Barbizon school.
Where do you think the path goes?
Notre-Dame de Paris
Charles Soulier photographed the cathedral after Victor Hugo's novel made it famous. The book The Hunchback of Notre-Dame had made people care about old churches.
How can a story make people care about a building?
Ornamental Sculpture, Paris Opera
Photographers Louis-Émile Durandelle and others recorded the decorations of the new Paris Opera house, which Napoleon III ordered. The photo shows the carved stone before it was set in place.
Why record each carving before it was put up?
Study of a Birch Tree, Barbizon
Constant Famin photographed a birch tree at Barbizon, where painters came to work from nature. Famin worked as a photographer only for a short time.
What do you notice about the bark?
Pont-de-Buis
Jules DuClos photographed a small town in Brittany when the railway arrived in stages. The tracks changed how people traveled.
How would a railway change a small town?
Man on a Horse
Nadar photographed a man on a horse in the 1860s. Portraits of riders had a long history in painting, and early photographers borrowed the idea.
Why did riders pose with their horses?
The Domes, from the Sentinel Domes, Yosemite
Carleton Watkins hauled a huge camera and glass plates into Yosemite in 1860 to photograph the valley. His pictures helped convince Congress to protect it in 1864.
Why would pictures help protect a valley?
Silenus Holding the Child Dionysus
Charles Soulier photographed a Roman marble statue in the Louvre of an old satyr holding the baby god Dionysus. Photographs of statues let people see art without traveling.
What do you think the old man is feeling?
